Avalanche Bulletin


Updated on 2026-02-20 17:00:00 MST, valid until 2026-02-21 17:00:00 MST.
Valid for: Crawford-Flathead-Lizard-Moyie-St. Mary.

    
Summary
Storm snow has added load to a complex upper snowpack creating touchy avalanche conditions. Stick to lower angle terrain with no overhead hazard.

Continue to make conservative terrain choices while the storm snow settles and stabilizes.Keep your guard up at lower elevations. Storms slabs have been reactive at all elevations.Keep in mind that human triggering may persist as natural avalanches taper off.Storm slabs in motion may step down to deeper layers resulting in large avalanches.

Problems
Problem 1: Storm slab.Recent storm snow will likely remain reactive as it settles. Cold temperatures may prolong its reactivity, specifically where it has formed over a crust or is affected by the wind.Problem 2: Persistent slab.Recent storm snow will likely remain reactive as it settles. Cold temperatures may prolong its reactivity, specifically where it has formed over a crust or is affected by the wind. Problem 1: Storm slab.There is a weak layer of surface hoar/crust/facets in the upper snowpack. This layer is spotty, but most likely areas to trigger it are on north-facing terrain, which were most recently reactive in the Flathead.Problem 2: Persistent slab.There is a weak layer of surface hoar/crust/facets in the upper snowpack. This layer is spotty, but most likely areas to trigger it are on north-facing terrain, which were most recently reactive in the Flathead.

Further Detail
Avalanche Summary A cycle of natural, human, and explosive triggered storm slab avalanches up to size 2 occurred on Tuesday and Wednesday in the Lizard Range. In the Flathead and St Mary's, there have been reports of several remotely triggered (from a distance of 100+ m) storm and persistent slab avalanches up to size 3. Some have had very wide propagations and were 50-60 cm deep. There was an avalanche fatality in the Matheson Creek area on Tuesday. See this MIN report for more details.
Snowpack Summary Roughly 50 cm of storm snow has developed touchy storm slabs over an upper snowpack that is variable and contains two distinct weak layers:50 cm deep, there is a supportive crust on south-facing terrain. On north-facing terrain, this crust is breakable or absent.Between 60 and 100 cm deep, a persistent weak layer of crust/facets with spotty surface hoar is present.The persistent weak layer is becoming less reactive, but continues to produce sporadic avalanches, particularly on north aspects where a supportive crust is absent and in less-travelled areas like the Flathead. Recent storm snow has increased the load on these layers.
Weather Summary Friday NightMostly clear skies. 10 to 20 km/h west ridgetop wind. Treeline temperature -13 °C.SaturdayMostly sunny. 10 to 20 km/h south ridgetop wind. Treeline temperature -10 °C.SundayMostly sunny. 20 to 50 km/h south ridgetop wind. Treeline temperature -7 °C.MondayMostly cloudy. 5 to 10 cm of snow. 40 to 70 km/h southwest ridgetop wind. Treeline temperature -4 °C. More details can be found in the Mountain Weather Forecast.

title: MVP’s Mountain Weather Update
text:
Lakeman’s Lookout
The following snippet is taken from the Mountain Forecast section of FAR’s website. Bear in mind that it will be up to 24 hours old by the time you read it! Many thanks as always to Ron Lakeman for his hard work.



Mountain Weather Report


ISSUED: Friday February 20, 2025 11:00 MST

SYNOPSIS: An upper ridge of high pressure will shift eastward across southern BC for dry, partly cloudy conditions today and Saturday. Greater cloud cover is expected late Saturday night as patchy moisture begins to drift northeastward from a large upper low pressure approaching the south coast-coastal Washington. A tightening pressure gradient supports increased wind at times tonight through Saturday night.

FREEZING LEVEL: Surface.

FERNIE ALPINE RESORT FORECAST (1615 metres):

TODAY: Morning fog patches, otherwise sunny with cloudy periods. High near -7.

TONIGHT: Clear with cloudy periods and possible fog patches. Increasing wind overnight. Low near -14.

SATURDAY: Possible morning low cloud and fog, otherwise sunny with cloudy periods. Windy at times. High -5 or -6.

SATURDAY NIGHT: Clear with cloudy periods during the evening, increasing cloud overnight. Windy. Low near -10.

OUTLOOK:

SUNDAY: Mainly cloudy with a slight chance of flurries. Windy. High near -2. Occasional snow Sunday night, light to moderate accumulation possible. Low -3 or -4.

MONDAY and MONDAY NIGHT: Cloudy with a few flurries or occasional snow, light to moderate accumulation possible. High 0 or -1. Low -1 or -2.

TUESDAY: Cloudy with a few flurries or occasional snow during the morning, 60% chance of afternoon flurries. High 0 or -1. Low near -4.

CONFIDENCE/DISCUSSION: Fair to good confidence today through Saturday night, fair Sunday and Sunday night. Poor to fair confidence Monday onward. Limited moisture should drift over the area of high pressure for a few bands of cloud or cloudy periods late today, tonight and Saturday. A developing temperature inversion and trapped low level moisture could also result in patchy low cloud/fog at times. The timing, moisture content and especially the positioning of a series of Pacific systems Sunday night through Tuesday are all questionable. The guidance is variable however it all currently suggests at least a light accumulation of snow Sunday night. Some computer models are trending the majority of the snow just south of Fernie Monday, Monday night and Tuesday. Other solutions suggest a moderate to heavy amount of snow is possible, more changes are likely.

 

Ron Lakeman.
